newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin returns to Kremlin after heart surgery.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin returns to Kremlin after heart surgery.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin returned to the Kremlin on Monday, seven weeks after a major operation on his heart, and promised Russians that things would get better next year.
The president's motorcade, a long column of limousines and security vehicles, rolled through the Kremlin's Borovitsky Gate soon after 9.30 a.m. (0630 GMT).
"The coming year will be better for Russia. That is the firm word of the president," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying when he reached his office.

Yeltsin told a television crew inside the Kremlin he was feeling fine. He said his priorities would include dealing with long and painful delays in paying pensions and wages and the need for military reform.
Yeltsin, 65, fell ill between the two rounds of Russia's presidential election and he had a heart bypass operation on November 5, four months after winning a second term in office.

He has been recovering since then in hospital and in government resthomes in the Moscow region and beyond it. He moved back to an official residence near Moscow on Sunday to be ready for his trip back to the Kremlin.
Interfax said Yeltsin would meet chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais on Monday and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Tuesday.
The president, speaking in his first televised address since the operation, said on Friday that Russia needed an active president, new ideas and courage, and he promised an energetic return to work.
"The doctors have done their job and now it is up to the president," he said. "There is no time for warming up. And also, this is against my character. If I work, I work in earnest."
Yeltsin looked much thinner than before his operation and he spoke in a firm and decisive voice.
But he appeared somewhat stiff and distant, lacking the spark which he displayed during his campaign for re-election in the first half of this year.
"In fact he is starting his second term as president with a delay of six months," Nikolai Svanidze, anchorman of the Zerkalo analytical programme on Russian Television, said on Saturday.
Yeltsin returns to a host of political and economic problems, including a fragile peace deal in the rebel region of Chechnya and prolonged delays in approving the Russian budget.

The draft 1997 budget is expected to be discussed by the State Duma lower house of parliament on a third and final reading at the end of the week, but it must still be approved by the upper house before Yeltsin can sign it into law.
"We can sigh with relief now, Boris Nikolayevich is returning," said Chubais, a hate figure for the communists who dominate the Duma.
Some reports had said the opposition in parliament was demanding Chubais's head as their price for backing the budget.
Yeltsin, who suffered two heart attacks last year, has had little time to run affairs of state closely this year.
An energetic campaign for re-election took most of his energy in the first half of the year, and he has been ill or recovering from surgery in the second half.
